title: Keep or discard what agents suggest
desc: An agent's changes appear on the slate as it works, as ghost notes everyone sees. Keep or discard each one in place, keep or discard all of an agent's at once, and undo any agent action.
terms: Keep or discard one change Keep or discard everything from one agent Pause every agent on a slate Let one agent edit directly What agents cannot do Troubleshooting
text: When an agent edits a slate, its changes appear on the slate as it works: see-through ghost notes and dashed lines, in the agent's color, on every screen. Nothing is saved until someone who can edit the slate keeps it. This covers every agent that edits through Slatebox: an assistant such as Claude or ChatGPT connected to Slatebox's MCP server, a script run with exec, an API call, and an agent someone invited onto the slate. The Slatebox agent, which works on tasks a person gave it, saves its work directly. Keep or discard one change 1. Watch the agent's named cursor. It moves to each ghost as it appears and says what it suggests, such as "Suggesting 2 new notes and 1 change". 2. Choose Keep on a ghost to save it. It becomes a real note for everyone, and one save in the slate's history. Your Keep is also one step of your own undo: Undo at the canvas's corner, or Ctrl+Z (⌘Z on a Mac), takes it back. If a teammate has changed the kept note since, or drawn a line to it, your undo leaves it as they left it and says so. 3. Choose Discard to remove it. Nothing is saved. A changed note shows the agent's version as a ghost over it. A removed note is marked until someone keeps or discards the removal. Keeping a line also keeps the new notes at its ends. People who can only view the slate see the ghosts and the cursor, without the buttons. Keep or discard everything from one agent Agents are listed after the people on the slate. Open an agent's chip to see: Item What it does --- --- The plan The steps the agent said it would take, ticked as it goes. Keep all Saves every change from this agent that is still waiting. A change that cannot land, such as an edit to a note someone deleted, is left out, and the chip says why. Discard all Removes every change from this agent that is still waiting. Activity The agent's recent actions in plain words, newest first. Undo Takes back one action that was kept. Only that action's changes go back, and only where nobody has changed them since, so another agent's work and your own later edits stay. An agent stays on the list while it works, while its changes wait, and for an hour after its last action. Pause every agent on a slate Choose Pause all agents on the agent list. Agents' edits on this slate are refused until someone who can edit chooses Resume agents . Changes already waiting stay, ready to keep or discard. Let one agent edit directly Where your Slatebox allows it, an agent's chip has an Edit directly switch for the person who brought the agent and for the slate's owner. With it on, that agent's changes save at once instead of waiting as ghosts. Each of its actions is still listed with Undo . Turn the switch off to go back to suggestions. Everyone else sees "Edits directly (set by Ada)" on the chip. Anyone who can edit the slate can choose Back to suggestions . On a self-hosted Slatebox, the operator allows the switch with settings.public.agents.editDirectly: true . What agents cannot do - No agent keeps suggestions, its own or another agent's. A person keeps them, or lets that agent edit directly. - An agent can undo only its own actions. While agents are paused, or an agent only suggests, it cannot undo or redo straight to the slate either. - Slate settings, such as the background or the slate's name, are not suggested. A person changes them, or an agent that may edit directly. Troubleshooting Symptom Fix --- --- Keep is missing on a ghost You can view this slate but not edit it. Ask its owner for edit access. A kept change was left out The note it changes is gone or was changed. The chip says which. Ask the agent again. Undo left some changes in place Someone changed those notes after the agent's action. Undo never overwrites a later edit. An agent's edits are refused Agents on this slate are paused. Choose Resume agents .

title: Choose your AI
desc: On a self-hosted Slatebox, connect any cloud provider with your key, or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint on your computer, your network or a host, and mix them per feature, for free. On Slatebox Cloud, AI comes with Slatebox Pro.
terms: Connect a model Choose a model for each feature When a model can't do something Who decides What is metered Where a model may be host.docker.internal http https localhost Reach a model on the same machine 127.0.0.1 Set the server's AI SLATEBOX_AI_KEY SLATEBOX_AI_CONFIG connections type url openai anthropic deepinfra model key tools vision images true false maxTokens use default chat generation presentation builtin SLATEBOX_AI_URL ownProviders off SLATEBOX_AI_OWN_PROVIDERS privateEndpoints SLATEBOX_AI_PRIVATE_ENDPOINTS Set it up with an agent slatebox.ai.get slatebox.ai.update slatebox.ai.check level me team server 403 on remove ai.update 200 effective ok reachable models yes no unknown message Troubleshooting SLATEBOX_KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY
text: On a self-hosted Slatebox, Slatebox uses the AI you choose: a cloud provider with your key, or any model behind an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, on your computer, your network or a host. Mix them freely, one model for conversation and another for images. Your own AI is free. On Slatebox Cloud, AI comes with Slatebox Pro credits and top-ups. Personal and team connections are for self-hosted Slatebox only. Profile → AI shows which AI each feature uses. Use your own keys · Pricing Connect a model On a self-hosted Slatebox: 1. Open Profile → AI and choose Connect a model . 2. Enter a Name (lowercase letters, digits and dashes, such as desk-model ) and choose a Type . 3. Fill in the fields for that type. 4. Choose Test connection . You see whether Slatebox reached the address, the key was accepted, the model answered and it called a test tool. Where an endpoint lists its models, choose one to fill in Model . 5. Choose Save . The connection appears under Yours , ready to choose for a feature. Type Address Model Key --- --- --- --- OpenAI-compatible endpoint The address up to /v1 , such as https://llm.example.com/v1 The model name the endpoint serves Only if the endpoint needs one OpenAI Filled in Required Required Anthropic Filled in Required Required DeepInfra Filled in Optional: empty follows each feature's default model Required Under the key, say what the model can do, where you know it: Calls tools and Reads images ( Yes , No or Not sure (try it) ), and Makes images . A capability you leave unknown is tried. Image generation needs Makes images ticked. Keys are encrypted with the server's key and never shown again; a saved connection says "key saved". To change a key, choose Change and enter the new one. Changing the address of a connection with a key needs the key again. Remove deletes the connection and its key at once. Choose a model for each feature Each feature has a menu under your connections. Set Default for every feature , then change only the features that need another model. Menu Covers The model must --- --- --- Default for every feature Every feature left Not set Do what each of those features needs Conversation and edits The conversation beside the canvas and the edits it proposes Call tools Drafts and layouts New drafts and layouts of a slate Call tools Presentation planning Planning the order and scenes of a presentation Call tools Reading images and diagrams Images you paste or attach in the conversation Read images Generating images Images AI makes for a slate Make images Each menu lists your connections ( Mine: ), your team's ( Team: ), this server's ( Server: ) and The AI this server provides . Which AI each feature uses , at the top of the tab, shows what answers each feature now and marks your own. Image search always uses the AI this server provides. When a model can't do something The feature stops, names the model and asks you to choose another. Slatebox never sends the request to another model instead. For example, with a default that cannot make images: Choose a model that makes images, or The AI this server provides , for Generating images . The same applies to a model that cannot call tools or read images. Who decides Slatebox looks for a choice in this order and uses the first it finds, for each feature: 1. Yours: your choice for that feature, then your default. 2. Your team's, set by a team admin under Your team's in Profile → AI . 3. This server's, set by an administrator under This server's (administrators) , or by the operator in the server settings. 4. The AI this server provides . Your choice always wins. On Slatebox Cloud, only the last two apply: nobody has personal or team connections there. On a self-hosted server, the one exception is a server whose operator turns off people's own AI ( SLATEBOX AI OWN PROVIDERS=off , or the People may use their own AI switch): everyone then uses the server's AI, and the AI tab says so. You can still remove what you saved. What is metered AI On Slatebox Cloud On your own server --- --- --- Your connections and your team's Not offered: own AI is for self-hosted Slatebox Free, with no limit from Slatebox. Your provider bills you directly, or nobody does for your own model. The AI this server provides Your Pro credits, then your balance Free, with no limit from Slatebox Image search Your Pro credits, then your balance Free, with no limit from Slatebox Pricing · Who pays for what on your own server Where a model may be Slatebox Cloud Your own server --- --- --- Your endpoints and your team's — (self-hosted only) Public addresses, your network and host.docker.internal , over http or https . Not the server itself ( localhost ) or a link-local address. SLATEBOX AI PRIVATE ENDPOINTS=off allows public addresses only. The operator's endpoints — Any address Requests never go to a cloud metadata address, and Slatebox follows no redirects. Each address is checked when it is saved and again on every request. Reach a model on the same machine Inside the Slatebox container, localhost is the container itself. A model server on the Docker host is at host.docker.internal , for example http://host.docker.internal:8000/v1 . - Mac: run the model server on the Mac itself, not in Docker: Docker on a Mac cannot use the Mac's GPU. Docker Desktop provides host.docker.internal . - Windows: Docker Desktop provides host.docker.internal . - Linux: start Slatebox with --add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway , and have the model server listen on the Docker bridge or on all interfaces, not only 127.0.0.1 . Set the server's AI An operator sets the AI everyone on a self-hosted server gets by default. One endpoint for every feature: SLATEBOX AI KEY is the endpoint's bearer token, if it needs one. For a mix, set SLATEBOX AI CONFIG to JSON instead. This one uses a model on the host for everything, and a cloud provider for reading and making images: Field Value --- --- connections Named connections. type is openai-compatible (with url ), openai , anthropic or deepinfra . model is the model name; key is needed for the three providers. tools , vision , images true or false : what the model can do, where you know it. Unset is tried; making images needs "images": true . maxTokens The longest answer, 256 to 200000. Default 16384. use Which connection serves default , chat , generation , presentation , vision and images . A value is a connection name, or builtin for the built-in AI ( SLATEBOX AI KEY without SLATEBOX AI URL ). ownProviders off keeps everyone on the AI set here. Same as SLATEBOX AI OWN PROVIDERS . privateEndpoints off keeps people's and teams' endpoints on public addresses. Same as SLATEBOX AI PRIVATE ENDPOINTS . A mistake in any of it stops the container with the reason. Keys go to the app's settings only, never to the log. To test every server connection: Each connection gets one line: reached, key accepted, model listed, answered and called tools. docker exec slatebox slatebox ai lists the connections and choices without keys. Administrators can also add server connections in Profile → AI . Set it up with an agent An agent reads, changes and tests AI settings with a token that has the ai:settings permission. Changing or testing a team's or the server's AI also needs ai:admin , and the token's owner must be a team admin or an administrator. Create the token in Profile → Developer access . To Exec HTTP --- --- --- Read the connections and what serves each feature, without keys slatebox.ai.get GET /api/v1/ai Add, change or remove connections, and choose them slatebox.ai.update PUT /api/v1/ai Test a saved or unsaved connection slatebox.ai.check POST /api/v1/ai/check A choice names a connection as me: , team: or server: , or is builtin for the AI this server provides. level is me , team or server . Levels me and team are for self-hosted Slatebox. Slatebox Cloud answers 403 to adding, changing, choosing or testing them, and to ownProviders on : "Own AI and call keys are for self-hosted Slatebox. title: Getting help
desc: Search the docs, ask the community at support.slatebox.com, share an idea, report a bug or write to us privately.
terms: Search the docs Ask the community From the app Report a bug well
text: Search first, then ask. Every question asked in the open helps the next person who has it. Search the docs Type in the search box at the top of any page, or press / to jump to it. Results show as you type; press Enter to see every result. Ask the community Go to support.slatebox.com. One search box looks through these docs and the community's questions at once. If nobody has asked yet, choose Ask a question . The community runs on GitHub Discussions, so you post with a GitHub account. The people who build Slatebox answer there too. Mark the reply that solved your question so others find it. You want to Go to --- --- Ask how to do something Ask a question Suggest a feature Share an idea Report something that does not work Report a bug Ask about your account, a payment or conduct, in private Contact us Report a security problem Our security policy, never a public post From the app Open the menu and choose Help and support . It opens these docs, the community, a bug report or the contact form. Report a bug fills in the app's version and your browser for you, and nothing else about you. Report a bug well 1. Say what you saw and what you expected instead. 2. List the steps that make it happen again. 3. Name where it happened: Slatebox Cloud, a self-hosted Slatebox (with its version), SlateboxJS in your app, or the MCP server. 4. Add a screenshot or the log lines. Remove keys, tokens and personal data first.

title: Invite an outside agent onto a slate
desc: Bring an MCP server such as Exa, Linear or GitHub onto a slate as a named agent. Ask it something and its answer appears as suggestions everyone on the slate sees. On Slatebox Cloud with Slatebox Pro or Slatebox Business; on a self-hosted Slatebox with an on-prem license.
terms: Invite an agent What it may see Ask it something https Who sees and does what Agents that need sign-in Remove an agent Troubleshooting
text: Invite an outside agent, any MCP server, onto a slate. Ask it something, and Slatebox AI turns its answer into notes and lines that appear on the slate as suggestions. Everyone on the slate sees the agent's cursor and its suggestions, and anyone who can edit keeps or discards them. On Slatebox Cloud, inviting agents is part of Slatebox Pro, and of Slatebox Business for every member of a Business team, for the person who invites them, on any slate they can edit. On a self-hosted Slatebox it needs an on-prem license from Slatebox, a flat yearly fee per install; there is no Slatebox Pro there. Slatebox Pro Invite an agent 1. On a slate you can edit, choose + Invite agent . 2. Choose an agent from the gallery, or paste an MCP server's address under Paste an MCP address and choose Next . Without Slatebox Pro or a Business team, the payment sheet opens in the app. Nothing else changes on the page. 3. If the server needs you to sign in, a window opens on the server's own sign-in page, or you paste a key or token it gave you and choose Use key . See Agents that need sign-in. 4. Read what it can do. Slatebox lists its tools in plain words: - Look things up : on to start. Clear any you do not want it to use. - Change things outside Slatebox : always off. Posting or changing things elsewhere is not available. 5. Set Name on your slate . A name cannot say Slatebox, admin, support or a person's name, or be the name of another agent on the slate. 6. Choose what it may see under It may see . The dialog says exactly what leaves Slatebox for each choice. 7. Choose Invite . The agent's cursor arrives on the slate and says hello. Consent is to each tool exactly as the server described it. If the server changes a tool later, the agent pauses before it calls anything, and you look at the change before asking again. What it may see Choice What leaves Slatebox when you ask --- --- Only what I ask What you type. What I ask, and the notes I select What you type, and the text of the notes you select. What I ask, and every note on this slate What you type, and the text of every note on the slate, including notes by others. Never: other slates, people's names or email addresses, comments, links or share settings. Ask it something Each invited agent is on the strip of people at the foot of the slate, as its own chip. Only the person who invited it can ask it, in either of two places: - Its chip. Choose the chip, type your request in its box and choose Ask . - Ask Slatebox. Put the agent's name after an @ anywhere in the message, such as @Exa how do others retry declined cards? or @GitHub open issues about sign-in . This works in the slate's own conversation, not in a board's (workshop) conversation. Its answer appears in the conversation under its own name, in its color, beside its mark. Your agents' names are also offered above the message box. 1. Ask it, such as "How do others retry declined cards?". 2. Watch the slate. Each part of the answer appears as ghost notes and lines in the agent's color, in the part of the slate you can see, and its cursor moves to them. The chip shows how many changes wait. Others on the slate who are looking elsewhere see a marker at the edge of their screen, such as "Exa is working →". Choose it to go there. 3. Keep or discard each ghost, or choose Keep all or Discard all on the chip. Each part is one action you can undo. Keep or discard what agents suggest Pictures in an answer are left out, and the ask box says so. Links are kept only when they are secure https addresses the server really sent. Who sees and does what Person Can --- --- The person who invited it Ask it, sign it in again, remove it, let it edit directly. The slate's owner Remove it. Anyone who can edit the slate See its cursor and suggestions, keep, discard and undo them. Anyone who can view the slate See its cursor and suggestions. A slate holds up to 8 invited agents, and up to 3 from one person. Agents that need sign-in Some servers, such as Linear and GitHub, need you to sign in. - A sign-in window opens on the server's own page. When you allow access, the window closes and the walkthrough carries on. Sign-in works only from the slate in your own signed-in browser. - The walkthrough names where your sign-in is sent, and what it lets Slatebox do. A GitHub sign-in reaches your public repositories and the names of your organizations, and is sent only to GitHub's own MCP server. - What the server gives Slatebox is stored encrypted for you alone. Nobody on the slate sees it, and it is sent only to that server. - A server that takes a key or token instead: paste it and choose Use key . Slatebox checks it with the server first. - If the server stops accepting the sign-in, the agent's chip says it needs sign-in. Choose Sign in again . - If your Slatebox Pro ends (and you are not on a Business team), the chip says so and asking is refused. Renew Slatebox Pro from the chip and the agent works again. Remove an agent Choose Remove on the agent's chip, then Remove again to confirm. Its waiting suggestions are discarded; what people kept stays. When no other slate of yours uses that server, its sign-in is revoked at the server and deleted. Troubleshooting Symptom Fix --- --- + Invite agent is missing You can view this slate but not edit it, or you are on a self-hosted Slatebox without an on-prem license. "That is not a web address" or a private-address message Use the server's public https address. Private and local addresses are refused. The agent paused because its tools changed Look at the changes the chip lists, then invite it again to choose. "Only … can ask" Only the person who invited an agent can ask it. Invite your own. Ask is grayed out Agents are paused on this slate. Choose Resume agents in the list of agents, then ask. The sign-in window was blocked Allow pop-ups for Slatebox and choose sign in again.

title: The shared library
desc: Find smart components, slates and presentations people built and shared, copy or branch any of them, build your own by chatting with Slatebox, and publish it for everyone. Free.
terms: Browse Use something from the library Build your own smart component The controls on the board Start from a branch Publish to the library Review submissions (administrators)
text: The library holds smart components, slates and presentations that people built on Slatebox and shared. Copy any of them, add a component to your slate, or branch off one and make it your own. Browsing, copying, branching and publishing are free; only AI turns use Pro credits or your balance. Browse Open Library in the menu, or go to app.slatebox.com/library. You do not need to sign in. To Do this --- --- Show one kind Choose Smart components , Slates or Presentations . Show one category Choose Plan , Decide , Meetings , Track or Map . Find something Type in Search the library . See what people use most Sort by Most used . Each item's page shows a live picture of it, who made it, what it was branched or forked from, its version and its license. A component also lists phrases to say in chat on any slate. The same library is public at slatebox.com/gallery. Use something from the library Item Choose You get --- --- --- Slate or presentation Open a copy A new private slate of yours. A presentation comes with its steps, ready to present. Smart component Add to a slate The board on a new slate, or beside the boards of a slate you pick. A slate holds up to 8 boards. Smart component Branch off A builder slate with your own copy of the board (see below). If you are not signed in, Slatebox makes you a guest first, so the copy is yours in this browser. Register before you rely on it from another device. Your copy says where it came from beside its name ("Copy of Launch plan by Ada Author"), which credits the original's author as its license asks. In a slate, Add to this slate in Ask Slatebox lists the same components, your own under Yours . Build your own smart component 1. Start from scratch: on a new slate, choose Build a board of my own in Ask Slatebox. Or open a component in the library and choose Branch off . 2. Say what the board should do, or pick a shape: Columns , Lists in lists , a tree, a timeline or a 2 by 2. Check the preview and keep it. The board grows on the canvas with each change you keep. 3. Set how it behaves. Say it ("Let Review hold 3"), or drag the controls drawn on the board: a lane's limit line, the arrows between lanes, a deadline, a freeze band. Each control makes the same change chat would. 4. Choose Save in the bar above the canvas. Give it a name, one line on what it does, and a category. It is saved to your library: add it to any slate from Add to this slate → Yours . A branch stays in the category of the component it came from, and says so in the bar. The controls on the board On a builder slate the controls are always drawn on the board. On any other slate they show on a board you select, if you can edit the slate. On Control Does --- --- --- A board of columns The limit line after a column's last slot Drag it, or use its − and +, to set how many cards the column holds. Hold it (or right-click) to switch between refusing and only warning. A board of columns The archive box on a column's header Makes the column an archive: it takes every card, whatever its limit, and deletes nothing. A board of columns The arrow between two columns Lets cards move only one way between them. A board of columns One column at a time Stops cards skipping columns. A board of columns The dashed column with a + Adds a column. A sales pipeline Each stage's − and +, and its padlock Sets the stage's limit, and whether a deal needs an amount to enter it. A launch or hiring plan Snap, the go-live line, what a slip does Moves by day or week; makes go-live a hard or soft line; says whether a slip pushes what waits. A nested board The ladder of levels, and − and + Sets how deep cards nest and how many a card holds. Point at a control, or select it with Tab , and it says what it does ("Make To do a bin that archives cards"). With the keyboard, then press Enter to tap it, the arrow keys to move it, or Delete to remove its rule. Anything else is set in chat, for example "Let Done hold 4"; the board lists every rule under "How this board behaves". Each change is saved at once as one step of your history: the canvas's Undo (Ctrl+Z, ⌘Z on a Mac) takes it back, and Redo makes it again. The next card you drag follows the new rule. Start from a branch Branch off gives you a copy of the component on a new builder slate. The bar says what it was branched from, for example "Branched from Retro (Meetings)". Change it as you like; the original is not changed, and its author is credited when you publish yours. Publish to the library What Where Choose --- --- --- A smart component The bar on its builder slate Submit to the library A slate Share Publish to the library , then Send for review A presentation The presentation settings, after you publish it Publish to the library , then Send for review Add a note for the reviewer if you like. Everything is reviewed before it is published; once it is, anyone can find it, use it and change their copy. Published items are shared under CC BY 4.0, and the credit to you is shown automatically. You need an account to publish: a guest is asked to register first. Follow your submissions in My library (app.slatebox.com/library/mine): Status What it means What you can do --- --- --- Submitted, In review A reviewer has it. Withdraw it, or write to the reviewer. Changes asked for The reviewer wrote what to change. Change it, then Send it again . Published It is in the library for everyone. Send an update; the published version stays until the update is approved. Withdraw the update takes back only the update. Take it out of the library removes the item. Not accepted The reviewer said why. Change it and send it again. When a reviewer publishes your item, asks for changes, turns it down or writes to you, you get a notice under the bell and an email, with their message and a link to My library. Open an item in My library to read its whole thread and to write back. The reviewer may make small changes before publishing, such as a clearer name or a tighter rule. They change a private review copy, never your slate. What is published is the reviewed copy. Saving a published component again changes nothing others see until your update is reviewed and approved. Review submissions (administrators) A server administrator opens app.slatebox.com/admin/library to see what is waiting, oldest first. 1. Choose Open for review . Slatebox makes a private review copy and opens it beside a review panel. 2. Ask Slatebox in the panel to refine it ("Tighten the rules", "Put it in Decide"), or change the copy yourself. Each proposal shows what would change before you keep it. 3. Choose Approve and publish , Send back with a message for the author, or Reject with the reason. What you approve is the review copy, with your refinements. Another administrator reviews what you submit yourself. If you are the server's only administrator, the review page offers Review it myself , and the thread records it. The refine chat is yours: the author sees what you decided and what changed, not what you asked the AI. To take a published item down, choose Take it out of the library ; copies people already made stay theirs. Agents and scripts can do every step too. Library API

title: Export and import Mermaid
desc: Write any slate as Mermaid text, or draw Mermaid as real notes and lines. Free on every slate, in the app, over HTTP and from an exec script.
terms: Export a slate mindmap flowchart subgraph Share a public slate's Mermaid gantt 404 Import Mermaid .mmd graph classDef class style click Export and import from an exec script slatebox mermaid.js exec.mjs exec.py name shareId importMermaid slatebox.slates.exportMermaid format auto styles start mermaid markdown formats warnings publicUrl slatebox.slates.importMermaid url kind notes frames lines created message Export and import over HTTP 200 201 What a round trip keeps o x v1.2 v1_2 _ Troubleshooting
text: Any slate you can open comes out as Mermaid text, and a Mermaid flowchart, mind map or Gantt chart goes in as real notes and lines. It is free, uses no AI, and works the same on Slatebox Cloud and on your own server. Export a slate 1. In the slate, open the slate menu and choose Mermaid . The Export tab shows the slate as Mermaid. 2. Pick a Format if you want another kind of diagram than the one chosen for you. Turn on Include colors to keep each note's colors. 3. Choose Copy Mermaid , Copy as Markdown , Download .mmd or Download .md . You can also open it from Export → Mermaid: export or import . A guest registers first, as for any export. Format What you get --- --- Automatic A mind map that is one tree as mindmap ; anything else as flowchart Flowchart Notes and lines. Direction comes from the way the lines run. Shapes, labels, arrowheads and dotted, thick or hidden lines are kept; a note drawn behind the notes it holds becomes a subgraph ; a workshop's lanes become subgraphs of their cards Mind map The tree under the root note Gantt chart Launch plans only. Each lane is a section, each card's points are days, and the chart starts today What Mermaid cannot say is listed as a warning, never dropped quietly. Mermaid has one broken-line style, so a dashed line is written as dotted. A line with an arrow only at its start is written from its other end. A line from a note to itself is left out. Share a public slate's Mermaid A public slate also has a plain-text address that always shows the slate as it is now. The Export tab shows it as Public Mermaid address . Address Returns --- --- /slates/your-share-id.mmd The Mermaid, as text/plain /slates/your-share-id.md The same, in a Markdown code block Add ?format=mindmap (or flowchart , gantt ) to choose the format. It needs no token. A private slate answers 404 . Import Mermaid 1. In a slate you can edit, open the slate menu, choose Mermaid , then Import . 2. Paste Mermaid, or choose Open a file for a .mmd file or a Markdown file with a Mermaid block. A line such as “Ready: a flowchart of 3 notes and 2 lines, in 1 frame.” says what will be drawn. 3. Choose Add to this slate or Open as a new slate . You get real notes and lines laid out in the diagram's direction. Subgraphs and Gantt sections arrive as frames. Everyone on the slate sees the diagram drawn. Mermaid Read --- --- flowchart and graph Every link form, chains, & , subgraphs, @{ shape: … } , classDef , class and style colors, and click links to web pages mindmap The tree, with its node shapes gantt Sections as frames and tasks as notes; durations stay in the note's text Any other kind Refused by name, and nothing is added One import takes up to 100,000 characters and 1,000 notes, counting frames. Export and import from an exec script Agents use the same two calls on every surface: the hosted MCP endpoint, the slatebox command and POST /api/v1/exec . Save the script as mermaid.js : Preview it first. The Node.js and Python tabs use the exec.mjs and exec.py helpers from Run a script. The result holds the slate's Mermaid and what the import would draw; a preview saves nothing. Run it again without --preview (or with mode: "save" ) to create the new slate. Leave out name and pass shareId to importMermaid to add the diagram to a slate you can edit. title: Agents on the canvas: suggestions, video notes and invited agents
desc: An agent's canvas edits are live suggestions people keep or discard. Read, keep, discard and undo them, add video notes, and (on Slatebox Cloud) invite and ask outside agents, from the API, exec or MCP.
terms: How an agent's edit lands edit_slate slatebox.slates.applyOperations 202 revision outcome suggested saved suggestion.actionId add update remove link unlink state pending update_slate Read and decide suggestions get_slate slates.get decide_suggestions suggestions.decide decision keep discard undo actionId itemIds confirmation_required itemId Video notes lookup_media media.lookup add_media_note slates.addMedia x y notice Invited agents list_invited_agents connectors.list discover_agent connectors.discover use_agent_key connectors.useKey invite_agent connectors.connect ask_invited_agent connectors.call view remove_agent connectors.disconnect 429 Troubleshooting
text: When an agent edits a slate's canvas, the edit is not saved: it appears live on the slate as suggestions for people to keep or discard. This page lists the calls that read and decide those suggestions, add video notes, and invite outside agents. Each call is the same on every surface, with the same checks: an HTTP route, a method in the exec client, and a typed tool on Slatebox's MCP server. How an agent's edit lands POST /api/v1/slates/{shareId}/operations ( edit slate , slatebox.slates.applyOperations ) from an agent's token answers 202 with outcome: "suggested" . Nothing is saved and revision is unchanged. Field Meaning --- --- outcome suggested : shown live on the slate, waiting for a person. saved : a person lets this agent edit directly, so it saved. suggestion.actionId The suggestion, as include=suggestions lists it. suggestion.items[] One item per change: add , update , remove , link or unlink , each with its state ( pending until someone decides). operations[].ids The new notes' ids. They work in your next edit, so you can connect, change or take back your own waiting notes. - People who can edit the slate keep or discard each item, or all of an agent's at once. Each kept action can be undone on its own. - Slate settings ( update slate ) are not suggested: the call answers 409 needs direct edit . - When people pause the slate's agents, an agent's edit answers 423 agents paused . - The Slatebox agent, working on a task a person gave it, saves directly. Agent tasks Keep or discard what agents suggest shows what people see. Read and decide suggestions Request Tool Exec Does --- --- --- --- GET /api/v1/slates/{shareId}?include=suggestions get slate slates.get Reads the slate with what agents suggested: what waits, and what became of each agent's recent actions POST /api/v1/slates/{shareId}/suggestions/decide decide suggestions suggestions.decide decision is keep , discard or undo , for one actionId ; itemIds picks some of its items - Deciding needs edit access to the slate and slates:write . - Only people keep suggestions. An agent's keep answers 403 people only , for its own suggestions and for any other agent's. - An agent can undo only its own actions. Undoing another agent's action answers 403 people only . - In an exec script, a keep or undo is held for the person to confirm, because it can remove notes ( confirmation required ). Exec - A kept item that cannot land, such as a change to a note someone deleted, is refused with its reason; the rest are kept. - undo takes back only what that action changed, and only where nobody changed it since. left[] says what stayed and why. Discarding one action over HTTP: The answer lists discarded[] , each with its actionId and itemId . Video notes Request Tool Exec Does --- --- --- --- POST /api/v1/media/lookup lookup media media.lookup Reads a YouTube, Vimeo or Loom address: { media, found, notice? } , with the title, author and a poster stored by the app POST /api/v1/slates/{shareId}/media add media note slates.addMedia Adds a video note. x and y place its top-left corner (320 by 180); without them it goes beside the slate's notes - Both need slates:write ; adding needs edit access to the slate. - Added by an agent, the note is a suggestion like any canvas edit ( 202 , outcome: "suggested" ). Added by a person, it saves. - Only YouTube, Vimeo and Loom addresses are video notes. Any other address answers 400 not a video . - Slatebox asks only each host's own oEmbed address, and fetches the poster only from that host's picture server. A host that shares nothing still gets a note with its play button, and notice says what was missing. - A person may look up 60 new videos an hour. A video already looked up does not count. Add a video to a slate shows the note in the app. Invited agents On Slatebox Cloud, a person with Slatebox Pro, or on a Slatebox Business team, can invite an outside MCP server onto a slate they can edit, as a named agent. A self-hosted Slatebox serves these routes only once an on-prem license switches them on (there is no Slatebox Pro there); without one they are not there. Request Tool Exec Does --- --- --- --- GET /api/v1/slates/{shareId}/agents list invited agents connectors.list The slate's invited agents, who invited each, and (for your own) the tools they may use POST /api/v1/slates/{shareId}/agents/discover discover agent connectors.discover Reaches a server's address and says what it can do, or how to sign in to it POST /api/v1/slates/{shareId}/agents/key use agent key connectors.useKey Gives Slatebox a key or token for a server that takes one, kept encrypted for you alone POST /api/v1/slates/{shareId}/agents invite agent connectors.connect Invites it: its name, the tools it may use (each with the hash you agreed to) and what it may see POST /api/v1/agents/{connectionId}/ask ask invited agent connectors.call Asks it. Its answer lands as suggestions: { items, actions, saved, say, left } . Send view (the part of the canvas you can see, in slate units) and its notes land there POST /api/v1/agents/{connectionId}/remove remove agent connectors.disconnect Removes it and discards what it still has waiting - On Slatebox Cloud, discovering, signing in, inviting and asking need Slatebox Pro, or a seat on a Slatebox Business team, for the person who invited the agent, checked on the server. Without it they answer 402 pro required . - On a self-hosted Slatebox whose on-prem license has ended, they answer 403 enterprise locked . - Only the person who invited an agent can ask it ( 403 inviter only ). The inviter or the slate's owner can remove it. Everyone who can read the slate sees it. - Signing in to a server that needs it happens in the slate, in your own signed-in browser. There is no route or tool for it, so no sign-in link can be passed to someone else. - A token reaches only slates its own account can open. A link to an unlisted slate does not count. - These calls reach outside servers, so each account can make 20 of them a minute, and 3 at a time. Over that they answer 429 . - When people pause the slate's agents, asking answers 423 agents paused before anything is sent to the outside server. - A slate holds up to 8 invited agents, and up to 3 from one person. - Keep, discard and undo what an invited agent suggests with suggestions.decide , like any agent's. Invite an outside agent onto a slate Troubleshooting Symptom Fix --- --- 202 with outcome: "suggested" Your edit is waiting for a person on the slate. Read it back with include=suggestions . 403 people only Only people keep suggestions, and an agent undoes only its own actions. Ask a person on the slate. 423 agents paused People on the slate paused its agents. Ask one of them to resume agents. 409 needs direct edit Slate settings are changed by a person, or by an agent a person lets edit directly.

title: Exec: how agents work with Slatebox
desc: Agents work with Slatebox by writing one short script against a typed client. Every call in it is checked as if you made it yourself.
terms: exec slatebox describe Why Slatebox uses exec Where your script runs exec_unavailable 127.0.0.1 Host Origin Why the server runner is sealed eval run What every call keeps idempotencyKey Saves that wait for confirmation details.confirmationId details.reasons SlateboxError confirmation_required confirmation confirm Limits truncated auditDays settings.selfHosted.exec Connect an agent SLATEBOX_API_TOKEN SLATEBOX_BASE_URL Local package over stdio Local package over HTTP Your Slatebox's MCP endpoint Your own code The CLI The exec tool intent code await return mode save preview preview_unavailable status completed failed result logs error usage details query methods insufficient_scope unknown_method Example scripts expectedRevision revision invalid_request slate_changed no_match Conversation requests on the canvas Use exec over HTTP 200 400 401 429 503 Audit and retention
text: An agent works with Slatebox through exec : it writes a short JavaScript or TypeScript program and runs it. Inside the program, slatebox is a typed client with one method for each thing your token may do. A second tool, describe , returns the method list, the full types and three worked recipes. exec and describe are listed on every Slatebox surface. The client is generated from the action registry that serves the HTTP API, so each new Slatebox action becomes a client method with no hand-written tool. On MCP, the server also lists one typed tool per client method, generated from the same contract, for assistants that pick one tool per task; each runs as an exec script of one call. Connect an assistant Why Slatebox uses exec A program can read a slate, decide and save one change in a single step, with no round trip through the model between calls. The runner is not what keeps your slates safe. The checks on every call are. Where your script runs Slatebox uses no external sandbox service. Where a script runs depends on who owns the machine. Surface Where the script runs What it can reach --- --- --- The local package over stdio ( slatebox-mcp ) or --http , and the CLI ( slatebox exec ) On your computer, in your own process, with no sandbox Everything you can reach, plus the client POST /api/v1/exec and slatebox exec --remote In the sealed runner inside the Slatebox app Only the client The hosted MCP endpoint ( POST /mcp on your Slatebox) In the sealed runner Only the client The side conversation on a canvas In the sealed runner, for that one slate Only the client, and only writes to that slate A self-hosted Slatebox ( ghcr.io/slatebox/slatebox ) In the sealed runner inside the image Only the client On your machine the script has your rights, like any script you run. It never receives your token, but without a sandbox a determined script can find it, or call /api/v1 directly and skip the exec rules. Your agent host's approval prompt for exec is your check. The package runs the script in a child process only so it can stop a stuck script after 30 seconds and keep its output off the MCP stream. Your instance applies the rules. Before a local run sends anything, the package asks GET /api/v1/instance whether the instance runs exec. Against an instance that does not run exec, the package stops before the script's first call and saves nothing ( exec unavailable ). Slatebox Cloud and the self-host image run exec. --http listens on 127.0.0.1 only, refuses requests whose Host or Origin is not loopback, and accepts only the token it was started with. That keeps a web page you visit from running code in your process. On Slatebox servers agent-written code never runs inside the Slatebox app process. It runs in QuickJS, which has no network or file API, inside a separate child process with no environment and no credentials. Every call passes back through the app's checks. Why the server runner is sealed Each layer needs its own bug to cross. Layer Holds against Does not hold against --- --- --- QuickJS guest. QuickJS compiled to WebAssembly, with frozen built-in prototypes Any access except the client: no network, file, environment, module, timer or eval API A bug in QuickJS or the WebAssembly runtime. QuickJS is not audited Child process. Empty environment and Node.js permission flags Reading app secrets, writing files, starting processes, loading native add-ons, exhausting the app's memory Opening a network socket after an escape from QuickJS: on Node.js 24, which Slatebox runs, the permission flags cannot deny the network. The database needs a password the child does not have Action registry. Every client call is checked as the caller Everything you may not do — The registry is the authority; the sandbox is defense in depth. The runner is the open-source run package (2.1.13, Apache-2.0), installed with the app. Your code is not sent to any other service. What every call keeps A call from a script is the same request as a direct HTTP API call and passes the same checks: - Scopes and sharing. Your token's scopes and your current access to each slate. A read-only collaborator can read; editing needs write scope and edit permission. - Revisions and workshop rules. A move a person could not make on the canvas is refused in a script too, with the same reason. - Preview and save. Put mode: "preview" in a write's input, or run the whole script with mode: "preview" . - Rate limits. Each call counts against your token's limit. - Idempotency. Each write's key is derived from the run's idempotencyKey . Rerun the same code with the same key and saved writes replay. A rerun that sends a different input at the same step is refused with 409 idempotency conflict ; earlier saves stay. - Audit. Every run is recorded (see Audit and retention). Scripts also have three limits of their own: - Token management is unreachable. Scripts cannot list, create or revoke tokens. - Call caps. At most 64 calls per script. - Some saves wait for you. See the next section. Saves that wait for confirmation A save is held, not made, when the script: - deletes notes or connectors, a slate or a comment, or withdraws an invitation; - rewrites the text of more than 10 existing notes in all (the count is kept for the whole script, so 8 notes on each of two slates are held); - changes or deletes existing notes or connectors on a slate someone else owns, or edits a map there. Slatebox does not yet record who wrote each note, so on your own slate a teammate's notes count as yours; - shows content to more people than the slates it read (for example, copying a private slate's text onto a public one); - grants access, such as creating an invitation link. These rules hold exec runs ( slatebox exec , POST /api/v1/exec , the MCP exec tool and every typed tool) and a token's direct API calls alike. A direct call that is held, such as a DELETE /api/v1/slates/{shareId} or a POST /api/v1/slates/{shareId}/operations that removes notes, answers 409 confirmation required with details.confirmationId and details.reasons , and saves nothing. To go ahead, send the same request again with the Slatebox-Confirm header set to that id and the same Idempotency-Key . Your own changes in the app are never held. A held call throws SlateboxError with code confirmation required . Calls before it have saved. The result has status: "confirmation required" and a confirmation with an id, an expiry and the reasons. To go ahead, run the same code again with confirm set to that id and the same idempotencyKey . A confirmation works once, for that code, for 10 minutes. Where you run exec Who confirms --- --- An MCP client The agent calls exec again with confirm . Most hosts ask you first, because exec is marked as a tool that changes data The CLI You: answer Save anyway? [y/N] , or pass --confirm ID The side conversation You: Keep changes confirms, and the preview shows the reasons POST /api/v1/exec Your application A direct API call Your application, with the Slatebox-Confirm header An agent you allow to run exec without asking can also confirm without asking. The rule is a speed bump with a record, not an approval system. Limits Limit Value --- --- Run time 30 seconds CPU time in the sealed runner 10 seconds Memory and stack in the sealed runner 32 MiB and 1 MiB Code size 64 KiB Calls per script 64 Calls in flight at once 4 Input and output per call 256 KiB and 512 KiB Operations per script, summed over its plans 200 Notes created per script 200 Note text rewrites in one script before confirmation 10 Returned result 40,000 characters of JSON, then cut and marked truncated Logs 16 KiB Runs at once on the server 2 per app process and 1 per account; another run gets 429 exec busy Audit retention 30 days On your machine the run time, call count, result and log limits apply; CPU and memory are not capped. A self-hosted operator can change any of these numbers, including auditDays , in settings.selfHosted.exec . Exec has no on/off switch: to stop

Shared caches keep a list or an item for at most a minute, so an item taken out of the library stops being served soon after. Answers to a token are never cached. An item that is not published answers 404 to everyone but its author and reviewers. Each person has a daily allowance: 10 submissions, 200 saves, 50 new builder slates, 100 copies and 100 messages in review threads. Past it the answer is 429 ( submit limit for submissions, library limit for the rest) with a sentence saying when to try again. Browsing has no allowance. Use an item from a script Each endpoint is a method of the exec client ( slatebox.library. ) and a typed MCP tool ( list library , get library item , use library item , branch library component , save library draft , submit to library and the rest). text: One command installs Slatebox on this computer, a Linux server or a Kubernetes cluster: Pick a team address and sign in; Slatebox runs at https:// .slatebox.team with no DNS, ports or certificates. It asks a few questions, shows a plan of everything it will write and run, and installs once you say yes. The short version: Run your own Slatebox You get the address with HTTPS and live collaboration, a Slatebox that starts on boot, daily backups, and your key encryption key kept in one private place. The installer ends with a one-time setup link: open it to create the first account, the server administrator. Nobody can sign up before that. Your own Slatebox is free, and its AI is whatever you connect, or none. Who pays for what on your own server Would rather not run anything? Use Slatebox Cloud. Install with one command Pick where Slatebox runs. You need Node.js 22.13 or newer where you type the command, and Docker where Slatebox runs. Where What you get --- --- This computer (Docker) A team address, https:// .slatebox.team , or your own domain. --local keeps it on http://localhost , the first free port from 7070. The port is published on 127.0.0.1 only; --listen 0.0.0.0 opens it to your network. Files in ~/.slatebox/installs/ / . Remote server Root or passwordless sudo over SSH. A team address with --team-address , or with --domain , HTTPS with automatic certificates (point DNS at the server, open ports 80 and 443). Without either, http:// :7070 . Files in /opt/slatebox , owned by root. Docker is installed only with --install-docker . Kubernetes kubectl and your current context; a context whose name looks like production must be named with --k8s-context . Namespace slatebox . One StatefulSet with a volume, a Service, the Secret -env , a backups sidecar, and an Ingress or Gateway API HTTPRoute with --route ingress or --route gateway . Files only A compose file, Kubernetes manifests or a Helm chart for GitOps, with placeholders where secrets go. - Nothing changes before the plan is shown. On a server or a cluster nothing changes without a yes. - The install waits for health. If it fails, the previous state is put back (exit 5). - Running it again with the same answers changes nothing. --name keeps several installs side by side. - No questions, from a script or a coding agent: npx slatebox install --team-address acme --yes . - Flags for every question: npx slatebox@latest --help . Let an agent install it Give your coding agent the brief, or copy this page's agent prompt: The agent writes an answers file, shows you the plan and installs only after your yes. An agent never gets a question on screen: a missing answer is exit 3 with each question, its choices and the flag that answers it. With --json , each line is one event ( plan , step , done , error ). The last line, done , carries address and secretsFile . Exit Meaning --- --- 0 Done, or nothing to change 2 Bad flags or answers; the error event lists each field 3 An answer or a confirmation is needed and nobody can be asked 4 A precondition failed: no Docker, no cluster access, CPU too old, port taken, image unavailable, key encryption key missing 5 The change failed its health check and was rolled back 6 The rollback failed too; the error event lists the commands a person must run 7 Canceled --yes , --install-docker , --new-encryption-key , --delete-data and --confirm count only when typed on the command line, never from the environment or an answers file. Your own domain A team address needs nothing but Docker. For a company install, keep the address on your own infrastructure instead: Address Command What you need --- --- --- A team address npx slatebox install --team-address acme Docker. A Slatebox account to approve the claim. Team addresses Your own domain npx slatebox install --domain boards.example.com DNS pointed at the server and ports 80 and 443 open. Slatebox gets and renews the certificate. Your own proxy npx slatebox install --url https://boards.example.com A proxy that ends HTTPS and forwards WebSocket upgrades to port 7070. Behind your own proxy This computer only npx slatebox install --local Nothing more: http://localhost on a free port from 7070. To leave a team address for your own domain, run the installer again with --domain ; your data stays. Turn on single sign-on with --sso . Your own tunnel A tunnel in your own Cloudflare account works the same way as a team address. Create a tunnel there, route its public hostname to http://localhost:7070 , and give the container its token and address in a file only you can read: The token goes to the tunnel only, never to the app or the log. Choose the AI when you install Slatebox is not tied to any AI provider, and the installer never picks one. Answer None for now , or give any mix of cloud and local models: kind Needs --- --- openai , anthropic , deepinfra , openrouter , groq , together , mistral model and a key ollama , lmstudio model ; no key openai-compatible url and model of any OpenAI-compatible endpoint you run (a model server of your own, a company gateway); a key if it needs one - A key is never typed into a flag or an answers file. Give key=env:NAME , key=file:/path , or key=prompt (typed, hidden). It is stored with the other secrets. - An endpoint on localhost is reached from the container as host.docker.internal ; the plan says so. - An image that takes one AI connection at a time says so before anything changes when you give several. Change it later, from the computer that installed: Where the encryption key lives The installer makes SLATEBOX KEY ENCRYPTION KEY once. It encrypts the AI and call keys people save. text: Move your whole team between your own Slatebox and Slatebox Cloud with one command. You see a report of what arrives, and nothing is visible on the other side until you confirm. What you need Side You need to be Sign-in --- --- --- The side you move from A team admin Its access token, or the browser code for Cloud The side you move to The owner of your team there, or in no team yet Its access token, or the browser code for Cloud - Your own server: make an access token in Profile → Developer with Export everything my team owns and Move a team here . Put it in SLATEBOX API TOKEN , or paste it when the command asks (nothing shows while you type). Its address comes from the install this computer made, SLATEBOX BASE URL , or --from / --to . - Slatebox Cloud: the command prints a short code and opens your browser. Sign in and approve it on the page titled Move your team . The sign-in can only export your team and move a team in, and it ends after an hour. In a script, set SLATEBOX CLOUD TOKEN instead (an access token with the same two permissions). What happens 1. The command checks both sides first. If one says no, nothing is copied. 2. It shows the plan: the team, how many slates and people, and where it lands. You agree. 3. It exports everything your team owns, encrypted with a passphrase made for this move. 4. The other side reads it into a hidden team and answers with a report: slates, files, people, library items, and anything left out. 5. You confirm. The team goes live: - In no team yet: it becomes your team, and you are its owner. - As a team owner: it joins your team. Your brand kit and agent choices stay. 6. The command asks once: Send invitations to the other members now? Press Enter for yes. In a script, nobody is invited unless you add --invite (or --no-invite to say no ahead). 7. It asks whether to delete the archive from this computer. Press Enter to keep it. The command prints how to delete it later. The team stays where it was. Remove it there when you are ready. Invitations - Each person gets an email to set a password and claim their account. Nobody can sign in without that email. - Someone who already has an account on the other side gets an invitation to join instead. They sign in with that account and accept. Nothing changes for them until they do. If they are in another team there, they leave it first. - Addresses the old server never verified are not invited. Check each one, then invite it. - To invite later, use the move id the command printed: Limits and checks Nobody at Slatebox reviews a move into Slatebox Cloud. Instead: - A move holds up to 2 GB. - Each archive is checked as untrusted: new addresses for everything, private until you confirm, board rules off, no keys. - You can start up to 3 moves a day. - Each move is recorded for the server's administrators. What moves Moves Does not move --- --- Slates, boards and smart components Passwords Recent versions and comments Agent and call keys (add them again) Presentations and uploaded files Access tokens (make them again) The brand kit, with its logos Connected agents and integrations (connect them again) Your library items, sent to the other side's review queue People, as placeholders until they accept the invitation Board rules arrive switched off until a team admin reviews them. Published links get new addresses. Library items show in the library only after that server's administrators approve them. Other ways Command Does --- --- npx slatebox install --from cloud Installs a new server, then prints the steps to bring your Cloud team over after you create the first account npx slatebox export --out acme.sbxteam --passphrase prompt Writes a team export file npx slatebox import acme.sbxteam --to cloud --passphrase prompt Moves a team export file in --invite , --no-invite Answers the invitations question ahead --delete-archive , --keep-archive Deletes the encrypted archive in ~/.slatebox/moves/ after the move, or keeps it without asking --replace-waiting Discards a move already waiting on the other side, then starts again A move waiting for your confirmation is removed after 14 days. Moving the same archive twice keeps the first move. Versions Slatebox Cloud is updated first, so it reads exports from any older server. If your own server is older than the export, the move stops with update this server . Update it, then run the same command again. The archive is kept, so nothing is exported twice. The file format is open: see Team export format.

text: Let people sign in to your own Slatebox with their company account. The image includes Keycloak, an open-source identity server, which connects to your company's sign-in: a SAML 2.0 or OpenID Connect provider, or an LDAP or Active Directory server. Single sign-on is off by default, and Keycloak does not run while it is off. It is for Slatebox you run yourself. Turn it on Take a backup, then start the container again with SLATEBOX SSO=keycloak and the options you already use: On that start, Slatebox sets everything up by itself: - Keycloak runs inside the container, on the same address under /auth . - A realm named slatebox , a client for the app and a client for SCIM provisioning, each with a generated secret. - A first Keycloak administrator, admin , with a generated password. The log says where the admin console is: You get a Sign in with SSO button on the sign-in page. Passwords and guests keep working unless you turn on SSO only. Print every address you need (admin console, issuer, the redirect address for your provider, the SCIM endpoint): Sign in to the admin console Open https://boards.example.com/auth/admin/ and sign in as admin with this password: 1. Create your own administrator in the master realm: Users → Add user , then Role mapping → Assign role → admin . Give them a long password. 2. Sign in as that person and delete admin . The generated password is for the first sign-in only. 3. Choose the slatebox realm at the top left. Every setting below is in that realm. Slatebox keeps brute-force protection and sign-in events on in the master realm at every start, so password guessing is slowed and recorded. Once your company's sign-in works, close the console on the public address: start the container again with SLATEBOX SSO ADMIN=closed . /auth/admin/ and the master realm then answer "not found", and sign-in keeps working. To change settings later, start it without that option. Behind your own proxy, you can instead allow /auth/admin/ and /auth/realms/master/ only from your network. Add your company's sign-in In the slatebox realm, open Identity providers and add one. Register the Redirect URI Keycloak shows ( https://boards.example.com/auth/realms/slatebox/broker/ /endpoint ) with your provider. Your provider In Keycloak What to enter --- --- --- Microsoft Entra ID OpenID Connect v1.0 Discovery endpoint https://login.microsoftonline.com/ /v2.0/.well-known/openid-configuration ; client ID and secret of an Entra ID app registration with Keycloak's Redirect URI. Okta OpenID Connect v1.0 Discovery endpoint https:// .okta.com/.well-known/openid-configuration ; client ID and secret of an Okta web app integration. Google Workspace Google Client ID and secret of an OAuth client. Set Hosted domain to your company's domain. Any SAML 2.0 provider SAML v2.0 The provider's metadata URL or file. Give the provider Keycloak's SP metadata: https://boards.example.com/auth/realms/slatebox/broker/ /endpoint/descriptor . Any other OpenID Connect provider OpenID Connect v1.0 Its discovery endpoint, client ID and secret. Trust Email Slatebox accepts an SSO sign-in only with a verified email address, and uses it to find the Slatebox account. Keycloak treats a provider's address as verified only when Trust Email is on for that provider. Anyone who can choose their own address at a trusted provider can sign in as that address's owner. Provider Trust Email --- --- Okta, Google Workspace, your own directory On: your administrators set or verify the addresses. Microsoft Entra ID Off, unless it is a single-tenant app registration whose mail attributes only your administrators can set. The email claim is not verified. Otherwise set Email verified per person in Keycloak. Another SAML or OpenID Connect provider On only if it verifies addresses or only administrators set them. People who exist in Keycloak before their first sign-in Someone provisioned with SCIM, or made by hand, stops at "Account already exists" on their first company sign-in. For a provider with Trust Email on: 1. Set First login flow override to link by trusted email . Slatebox creates this flow; it links the person to the Keycloak user with the same address. 2. Set Sync mode to Force . Keycloak then takes the address from the provider at each sign-in and marks it verified. Without it, Slatebox refuses SCIM users. Do not use this flow for a provider with Trust Email off. To skip Keycloak's page and go straight to your provider: Authentication → browser flow → Identity Provider Redirector → settings, and enter the provider's alias as the default. LDAP and Active Directory 1. Open User federation → Add LDAP providers and choose the vendor. 2. Enter the connection URL ( ldaps://dc.example.com ), bind DN and password, and the users DN. Keep Edit mode on READ ONLY . 3. Turn on Trust Email . Without it, Slatebox refuses every directory user. 4. Use Test connection and Test authentication , then save. 5. On the first sign-in, Slatebox picks the account in this order: - the account already linked to this person; - the Slatebox account with the same address, if Slatebox verified that address itself or nobody can use the account yet (an unaccepted team invitation); - a new account with the name and address the provider sent. text: A team address is a free name for your own Slatebox, https:// .slatebox.team . You get HTTPS and live collaboration with no DNS, ports or certificates to set up. The installer prints a short code and offers to open your browser. Sign in to your Slatebox account, approve the code, and acme.slatebox.team is claimed for you. Slatebox starts and the installer prints the address once it answers, with a one-time setup link, https://acme.slatebox.team/setup/… . Open it to create the first account: you become the server administrator. Nobody can sign up before that, so the public address is safe to share from the start. The link works once and expires in 24 hours; slatebox setup-link prints a new one. How it works - The container connects out to Cloudflare through a secure tunnel. Cloudflare ends HTTPS and carries the app and live editing to it. - Nothing is opened on your machine or router. Only 127.0.0.1 is published on the host. - The container starts again when the machine does, and reconnects on the same address. - Your address is public; your slates are not. People still sign in or open a share link. - The tunnel takes uploads of up to 100 MB, more than Slatebox itself accepts, so uploads work as they do anywhere else. The install keeps one credential for the address, on the computer that installed: ~/.slatebox/installs/ /credentials.json , mode 0600. It can fetch the tunnel token again and give the address back, and nothing else. Names - 3 to 32 characters: a-z, 0-9 and hyphens. Case does not matter. - An account holds up to 3 team addresses. - Claiming a name needs a Slatebox account with a verified email. Rename, rotate and release Each claim, rename or reconnect is approved in your browser. desc: How Slatebox is versioned and released, which image your server runs, how to move to a new version and back, and how security fixes reach you.

text: Every part of Slatebox has its own version number, its own changelog and release notes for each version. A self-hosted Slatebox moves to a new version only when its admin chooses, after a backup, and goes back if the new version fails its health check. What has a version Part Published as Tag Notes --- --- --- --- The app and the self-host image ghcr.io/slatebox/slatebox:X.Y.Z vX.Y.Z Releases The installer and CLI npm slatebox slatebox@X.Y.Z Changelog The MCP server and its CLI npm slatebox-mcp slatebox-mcp@X.Y.Z Changelog The SlateboxJS engine npm slateboxjs vX.Y.Z in Slatebox/slateboxjs Changelog All of them follow Semantic Versioning: a major version changes or removes something people rely on, a minor version adds features, a patch fixes. Changelogs are written from the commit messages (Conventional Commits), one section per version. Each image is built and signed by GitHub from its release tag (cosign, with build provenance), for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64 . Slatebox Cloud always runs the newest build. Which version you run Installer 0.3.0 and later pin the newest published image by its digest, so every install of the same installer version runs the same bytes. To see the version: A server on 2.1.0 or later also shows it in Admin › Updates , with the newest release for your channel, and can update itself. An older install runs npx slatebox@latest upgrade once, after installer 0.3.0 is on npm, to get there. Move to a new version It takes a backup, starts the new image, waits for it to be healthy, and on a failure puts the previous image and the backup back. The plan shows the new image and the backup before anything changes. Upgrade without the installer Security fixes Security fixes go into the newest release of each part. Staying on the newest image is how you get them. Report a problem privately, as described in the security policy.
